How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The school has many platforms fx. Heico, übungen, moodle, müsli, heibox etc. There is no consistency about what is located where, and some of them dont even share login data.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Everything has to be done physically at the school or using a VPN with two-factor authentication. It requires a login to setup 2FA, but it requires 2FA to login. Took a long time to find the way through. Then a lot of documents needs to be signed, both online and physically at different offices. Not very streamlined.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: i think it would be possible to write erasmus coordinators.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer:
I managed in the end. It does requires registrations on multiple platforms. Much of the information about the course is different than what is presented on the website. Especially the correct weekly schedule was only available at the first or second lecture. So it was almost impossible to plan which courses to take up until a week or two into the semester. 

This would not be a problem, if the courses didnt have mandatory weekly assignments. The result is that students have to attend many classes for some weeks, until a proper schedule could be made.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Show up in person for everything. Dont trust the system and website. Write all professors directly. Also for things like schedule, requirements etc.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
Its a very old school way of doing university. The school has more focus on working hard than on learning. 

An example is the tuturial sessions. My classes had weekly mandatory assignments that was often quite difficult. The tuturial sessions were placed right after the hand-in deadline and right before the release of the next assignment. This meant that, at no point in the courses, was it possible to get any assistance from the tutors with the problems.

Instead of teaching and explaining things and guiding, students are expected to figure it out themselves. Then the school will tell them if they did it right or wrong (but you have to do it right otherwise you are not allowed to go to the exam). 

Another example is, if you hand in a file for a problem 3.1 as "name_lastname_problem_3." (that is, you forget the last 1), they will cut the points from your assignments. Generally small mistakes in practical things leads to large consequences. 

Final example: Many of the exams in my courses allowed no notes or other material. This means that the exams is all about memorizing. This might be subjective, but i dont think that memorizing is an important factor in understanding complex topics. 

My field is very much in programming, which means that most of the work done through the course and in the exercises is programming. Programming is very much a process of looking up names and functions and trial and error (like trying something, seeing that its not working, and then correcting it). The exams in my programming courses were all pen and paper, which meant the exam problems were widely different than what was taught in the course. The exams also included writing code but in pen and paper, which just does not make sense for the topic. 

So overall: The school focuses very little on making the students learn and explore, and much more on memorizing and producing reports, strongly punishing small errors. The level is not that high, theres just no teaching involved. Only presentations and deadlines.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level is not that high, but a lot of work is expected. Most of everything you do has to be handed in and graded which is very time consuming. So even if the problems are easy and you already know how to do them, you have to spent hours writing solutions and transfer it to a format that sufficient for a graded report.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
The style at host institution is very old school. You have to figure things out yourself, and if you dont you will be told that you are bad and might not be able to go to exams. 

It feels like the teachers think students are just lazy people who needs to be forced to do everything. Example: if a lecture is bad (that is: does very confusing lectures with unreadable handwriting and countless mistakes), many students decide not to show up because time is spent better learning from other sources. The fix to this: force students to show up. 

Comparing with UCPH theres a lot more teaching involved. The students learns through dialogue with the tutors and sometimes the professors, and staff seems to trust that you know what you are doing. But again, the scandinavian countries are also know for a flatter hierarchical structure, that Germany is not known for.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Optimization in Machine Learning and Vision. 

Generally any course that a "seminar". This is the only part where Heidelberg got it right. These courses are about reading scientific papers and presenting them to other students. Here dialogue and communication is essential, and you get a lot of presentations that are cutting-edge and more digestable than usual lectures.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Theres a lot of things you need to get when you arrive at an empty room, like duvets, sheets, clothes lamps etc. This ended up being more expensive than i though.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food can be very cheap. The canteen at uni can give you a full semi-healthy cooked meal for 2-5 euro. Going out is also very cheap (drinks and restaurants).

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The city has a great ESN (Erasmus student network). They host a lot of events and each ESN tutor seems to really care that all the international students gets a nice start of their semester.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Basically every sport, and a lot of smaller clubs. Its not difficult to find things to to. The difficult parts is finding free time to do them.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Go to the ESN events in the beginning, although it might be scary. People are really nice and interesting.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Heidelberg uni does not have holidays, except some days around christmas (but you get homework for this break). Weekends are mostly for catching up on courses, but most things are closed on sundays, so i would recommend exploring the nearby mountain forests.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy. But again, german and danish culture is not that different.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Just start talking to people in your classes/at sports. Everybody has no problem speaking english.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
The work mentallity is very different. People have no problem spending their nights studying and sleeping 4 hours each day. Makes it quite difficult to keep up with their level of productivity. It also makes it hard not just to follow their path and ending up ruining yourself. 

University students in germany are generally quite young, and many people are very dedicated students. This means that many university students havent done that many other things than studying, which contributes to the "young" feeling. Sometimes university is comparable to 2.G and 3.G in gymnasiet in Denmark.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The germans has a lot of systems, but in the end none of them really works. This means that if you want something done you just show up and talk to people. It can be frustrating in the beginning, but in the end its much easier. No more waiting for responses and filling formulas. Just show up and they will fix your problem and sign your papers.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
The workload is very intense, and theres not really any help to get. Would really try to take easy courses or less than 30 ECTS if possible. None of the locals do 30 ECTS semesters. Its not build for that.
Don't trust university websites information. Much of it is outdated anyways. The real information is given in the first few lectures of a course. So the first month is chaos because everybody is attending every class at the same time, trying to figure out what the schedule for each course is. Dont worry, thats apparently how its supposed to be. It will all settle down. If any doubt, write or talk to professors.
The city is very active and great for internationals. Try and find a way to get some free-time and you will be rewarded with great food/music/experiences of many different cultures. Try and find private housing perhaps in a WG with germans and people outside of your studies (
WG-gesucht.de
). This will open your circle of people broadly.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Interrail has an Erasmus pass, which gives you 6 travel days very cheaply. Perfect for a getting there and back, and perhaps a visit home or to neightbouring countries.

Kleinanzeigen has cheap used things.

The Mensa's of Heidelberg are really good and cheap for students. Dont worry about packing a lunchpack ever again.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting people from all over the world and hearing about their backgrounds and culture.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The workload. It was very difficult to find time to do things with many weekly written reports and loads of classes. Theres tons of opportunities to meet people, experience the area and do cultural things, but most weekends is spend at the library.
